items.title: Energy and AI (World Energy Outlook Special Report)
items.locator: Executive summary, p.14 (figures); Chapter 1, p.44, paragraph beginning 'Similar caveats hold' (quotation); p.46 on energy per task
items.quote: This lack of data makes it hard to estimate energy consumption for the field of AI as a whole
items.why: Source of the quotation and the figure. Data centres used around 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of world electricity, and the Base Case reaches around 945 TWh by 2030; these are all data centre use, not AI alone, and the report gives a range of 670 to 1,260 TWh across its cases. Says the size and implementation of most commercial models are not disclosed, so their energy use cannot be measured from outside. The PDF is the agency's own file on its download server; the report's web pages on iea.org refused an automated request (HTTP 403).

items.title: Engineering Responsible AI: foundations for environmentally sustainable AI
items.publisher: National Engineering Policy Centre (Royal Academy of Engineering, with the Institution of Engineering and Technology and BCS)
items.locator: PDF page 7, section on better data; foundational step 1 'Expanding environmental reporting mandates', PDF page 8
items.quote: a lack of clarity on the precise scale of AI’s environmental impacts currently hinders policymakers’ ability to forecast and prepare for future risks
items.why: The main UK professional statement. Says AI systems place demands on energy, water and critical materials and that the extent is often unclear; recommends mandatory reporting by data centres of energy, water, carbon and e-waste, and environmental sustainability in procurement guidelines for AI. Recommendations to government, not obligations on businesses.

items.title: AI Energy Council
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology; Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
items.locator: Section 'Role of the group' and list 'Key areas being discussed by the AI Energy Council'
items.quote: to address the growing energy demands of AI in the UK
items.why: Shows where UK policy stands: a council co-chaired by two Secretaries of State, with 'Sustainable AI' and energy demand forecasting among its topics. It is a forum; the page sets no duty on users of AI. No date is printed on the page; page metadata gives 4 September 2025.

items.title: UK Compute Roadmap
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section on AI Growth Zones, paragraph beginning 'Noting that AI infrastructure is enormously energy intensive'; section on the AI Research Resource, 'Security and sustainability by design'
items.quote: The government is committed to delivering AI Growth Zones sustainably, ensuring impact on energy, water and wider environmental systems are considered and minimised.
items.why: Government's own statement that AI infrastructure is 'enormously energy intensive', with a commitment to 'clear sustainability metrics' for public compute. A commitment about public infrastructure, not a rule for businesses. The page shows 'Updated 23 April 2026' and a banner that it was published under the previous government; page metadata gives first publication on 17 July 2025.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), Annex XI: technical documentation for providers of general-purpose AI models
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk (Commission's copy of the Official Journal text)
items.locator: Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(d) and (e) and the sentence that follows; read with Article 53(1)(a) and (5), Article 40(2) and Article 112(6) on the same site
items.quote: where the energy consumption of the model is unknown, the energy consumption may be based on information about computational resources used
items.why: The only binding energy rule found. Providers of general-purpose models must keep technical documentation including 'known or estimated energy consumption of the model', to give to the AI Office and national authorities on request (Article 53(1)(a)). Annex XII, the information owed to businesses that build on a model, has no energy item. This is the Commission's copy; the page says it uses the 'Official version of 13 June 2024', although the site's contents list shows a later Article 4a, so later amendments may not be fully reflected. EUR-Lex returned an empty page. No application date is stated here.

items.title: Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard
items.publisher: Greenhouse Gas Protocol (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development)
items.locator: Section 5.5, 'Category 1: Purchased goods and services', PDF page 40
items.quote: Products include both goods (tangible products) and services (intangible products).
items.why: Where bought-in AI sits in a carbon account. Category 1 covers the upstream emissions of purchased services, which is how cloud and AI services bought from a supplier are counted; the standard does not mention cloud or AI by name. Electricity for the organisation's own servers is Scope 2 (Scope 2 Guidance, section 5.3, read alongside).

items.title: Environmental Reporting Guidelines: including Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting guidance
items.publisher: HM Government (Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy; Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs)
items.locator: Chapter 2, section 'Should quoted companies report all their emissions?', printed page 39 (PDF page 39)
items.quote: You are not required to report on other emissions associated with inputs into your company (such as emissions from your supply chain)
items.why: Basis for the statement that UK reporting law does not reach bought-in AI. Statutory energy and carbon reporting covers a company's own fuel and purchased electricity; supply chain emissions are recommended, not required. The underlying rule is Schedule 7, Parts 7 and 7A of S.I. 2008/410 (paragraph 20D read alongside). Guidance dated 2019; applies to quoted and large companies only.

items.title: Power Hungry Processing: Watts Driving the Cost of AI Deployment?
items.publisher: Luccioni, Jernite and Strubell (ACM FAccT 2024); arXiv
items.locator: Abstract; section 4.1 of the paper (PDF page 6) for energy per 1,000 inferences by task
items.quote: multi-purpose, generative architectures are orders of magnitude more expensive than task-specific systems
items.why: Evidence that model choice changes the footprint. Measured energy for 1,000 inferences across 88 models: image generation used on average over 60 times more energy than text generation, and general-purpose models far more than task-specific ones for the same task. Limits: open models run by the authors on their own hardware; commercial services were not measured. Authors' open copy of a peer-reviewed conference paper.

items.title: Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP
items.publisher: Strubell, Ganesh and McCallum; Association for Computational Linguistics
items.quote: Authors should report training time and sensitivity to hyperparameters.
items.why: The paper that started the measurement of AI's energy cost, and the origin of the call for developers to report the resources a model needs so that later users can judge it. It concerns training research models in 2019; its emission estimates are dated and are not used in the brief.

items.title: Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) Specification, version 1.1.0
items.locator: Introduction, final two paragraphs; section 'Methodology summary' (SCI = (O + M) per R)
items.quote: users of this specification are strongly advised to request such data from their suppliers
items.why: A free method for turning an estimate into a rate (emissions per user, per call or per task) that can be tracked over time. Allows modelled estimates where real data cannot be had, and tells users to ask suppliers for it. The ISO page for ISO/IEC 21031 refused an automated request and was not read, so the relationship between the two texts is not confirmed here. Copyright line gives 2024.

items.title: ICT Sector Guidance built on the GHG Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard, Chapter 4: Cloud and data center services
items.locator: Chapter 4, 'Executive Summary: Cloud and data center services', printed page 4-4 (PDF page 120); section 4.6 on allocation
items.quote: a key question is how to allocate the GHG emissions of a data center to its various services and clients
items.why: The standard-setter's own method for working out a customer's share of a shared data centre's emissions, which is the problem a buyer of cloud AI faces. Limits: voluntary guidance dated July 2017, written before generative AI; it covers greenhouse gases, not water; it does not mention AI.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.publisher: Government Digital Service (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology)
items.locator: Principle 2 'You use AI lawfully, ethically and responsibly'; section 'Using AI safely and responsibly', sustainability bullet and practical recommendations
items.quote: You should understand and manage the environmental impact of the AI systems you are planning to use.
items.why: Government's own instruction to its departments: assess the environmental impact before development, weigh it against benefit, and judge suppliers' environmental credentials. It is the nearest UK official statement of what the criterion asks. Limits: guidance for the public sector, not binding on business; gives no measurement method.

items.title: Water use in AI and Data Centres
items.publisher: Government Digital Sustainability Alliance (published by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs)
items.locator: Section 1, introduction (PDF page 2); section on UK regulation and the transparency gap; strategic recommendations
items.quote: accurate measurement is foundational to targeted intervention and accountability
items.why: Covers the water side of the footprint for the UK, which the existing list lacks, and says the data to measure it is missing. Limits: written by an industry alliance convened by Defra and published on GOV.UK; it makes recommendations to government rather than stating policy; several figures are taken from secondary sources and were not checked here.

items.title: Directive (EU) 2023/1791 on energy efficiency (recast), Article 12: Data centres
items.publisher: European Union (Publications Office copy of the Official Journal text)
items.locator: Article 12(1) to (4); Annex VII lists the information
items.quote: to make the information set out in Annex VII publicly available
items.why: Binding EU rule that operators of data centres of at least 500kW installed IT power demand publish energy and sustainability information each year. It shows what a legal disclosure duty looks like where the UK has none, and is a source of supplier data for UK firms using EU-hosted services. Limits: not UK law; binds member states and operators, not customers; the duty is per data centre, not per AI service; later delegated acts on the rating scheme were not read.

items.title: The Large and Medium-sized Companies and Groups (Accounts and Reports) Regulations 2008, Schedule 7, Part 7A: energy and carbon report (unquoted companies)
items.quote: the annual quantity of energy consumed resulting from the purchase of electricity by the company for its own use
items.why: The binding UK rule behind the brief's statement that energy and carbon reporting covers a company's own energy use: gas, transport fuel and electricity bought for its own use. Energy used by a cloud or AI supplier on the company's behalf is outside it. Limits: applies to large companies only; Part 7A was inserted in 2018; the site notes revised text may not be fully up to date.

items.title: Making AI Less "Thirsty": Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models
items.publisher: Li, Yang, Islam and Ren; arXiv (accepted by Communications of the ACM)
items.quote: we provide a principled methodology to estimate the water footprint of AI
items.why: The main research source on AI's water use, with a method for estimating it; the brief keeps water in scope and the log recorded that no method had been read. Limits: arXiv copy of a paper accepted by a peer-reviewed magazine; the 2027 projection is a model estimate; examples drawn from US data centres.

items.title: Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale
items.quote: we find the median Gemini Apps text prompt consumes 0.24 Wh of energy
items.why: A supplier's measured energy, carbon and water per prompt in production, with the measurement boundary stated: the kind of supplier disclosure the criterion's third level relies on. Limits: preprint, not peer reviewed; written by the supplier about its own product; a median for text prompts only; excludes training; not comparable with other suppliers' figures without the same boundary.
